claim: P-loop nucleoside triphosphatases (NTPases) represent the most common protein fold that can comprise up to 18% of all gene products in a cell.
source: P-loop nucleoside triphosphatases (NTPases) represent the most common protein fold that can comprise up to 18% of all gene products in a cell.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Koonin et al., 2000; Lupas et al., 2001; Leipe et al., 2002; Ponting and Russell, 2002; Anantharaman et al., 2003; Söding and Lupas, 2003; Orengo and Thornton, 2005; Ranea et al., 2006; Wittinghofer and Vetter, 2011; Verstraeten et al., 2011; Alva et al., 2015; Wuichet and Søgaard-Andersen, 2015)

claim: P-loop NTPase domains apparently preceded the Last Universal Cellular Ancestor.
source: P-loop NTPase domains, which apparently preceded the Last Universal Cellular Ancestor, are found in translation factors, small GTPases, kinases, helicases, rotary ATP synthases, and many other ubiquitous proteins (Koonin et al., 2000; Lupas et al., 2001; Leipe et al., 2002; Ponting and Russell, 2002; Anantharaman et al., 2003; Söding and Lupas, 2003; Orengo and Thornton, 2005; Ranea et al., 2006; Wittinghofer and Vetter, 2011; Verstraeten et al., 2011; Alva et al., 2015; Wuichet and Søgaard-Andersen, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The P-loop fold is a 3-layer αβα sandwich, where the N-terminal β-strand is connected with the following α-helix by an elongated flexible loop typically containing the GxxxxGK[ST] sequence motif, known as the Walker A motif.
source: The P-loop fold, a variation of the Rossmann fold, is a 3-layer αβα sandwich, where the N-terminal β-strand is connected with the following α-helix by an elongated flexible loop typically containing the GxxxxGK[ST] sequence motif, known as the Walker A motif (Walker et al., 1982), see Figure 1.
evidence: Supported by citation to Walker et al., 1982 and reference to Figure 1

claim: The conserved lysine residue of the P-loop forms hydrogen bonds with β- and γ-phosphate groups.
source: The conserved lysine residue of the P-loop forms hydrogen bonds (H-bonds) with β- and γ-phosphate groups, while the next Ser/Thr residue coordinates the Mg2+ ion, which, in its turn, coordinates β- and γ-phosphates from the other side of the phosphate chain (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1A-C showing structural data

claim: The Ser/Thr residue following the conserved P-loop lysine coordinates the Mg2+ ion.
source: The conserved lysine residue of the P-loop forms hydrogen bonds (H-bonds) with β- and γ-phosphate groups, while the next Ser/Thr residue coordinates the Mg2+ ion, which, in its turn, coordinates β- and γ-phosphates from the other side of the phosphate chain (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1A-C showing structural data

claim: The Mg2+ ion coordinates β- and γ-phosphates from the other side of the phosphate chain.
source: The conserved lysine residue of the P-loop forms hydrogen bonds (H-bonds) with β- and γ-phosphate groups, while the next Ser/Thr residue coordinates the Mg2+ ion, which, in its turn, coordinates β- and γ-phosphates from the other side of the phosphate chain (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1A-C showing structural data

claim: The Walker B motif has the sequence pattern hhhhD, where 'h' denotes a hydrophobic residue.
source: Another motif typical for P-loop proteins is the Walker B motif with the sequence pattern hhhhD, where 'h' denotes a hydrophobic residue (Walker et al., 1982).
evidence: Supported by citation to Walker et al., 1982

claim: In P-loop NTPases, the aspartate from the Walker B motif either serves as a direct Mg2+ ligand or participates in the second coordination sphere of Mg2+ ion.
source: In P-loop NTPases, the aspartate from this motif either serves as a direct Mg2+ ligand or participates in the second coordination sphere of Mg2+ ion.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of P-loop NTPase structure

claim: Catalytic activity of P-loop NTPases typically depends upon their interaction with other proteins or domains of the same protein or RNA/DNA molecules.
source: Catalytic activity of P-loop NTPases typically depends upon their interaction with other proteins or domains of the same protein or RNA/DNA molecules; upon this interaction, activating Arg or Lys 'fingers' are inserted into the catalytic site (Bos et al., 2007), see Figure 1A.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bos et al., 2007 and reference to Figure 1A

claim: Upon interaction with activating partners, activating Arg or Lys 'fingers' are inserted into the catalytic site of P-loop NTPases.
source: Catalytic activity of P-loop NTPases typically depends upon their interaction with other proteins or domains of the same protein or RNA/DNA molecules; upon this interaction, activating Arg or Lys 'fingers' are inserted into the catalytic site (Bos et al., 2007), see Figure 1A.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bos et al., 2007 and reference to Figure 1A

claim: Gerwert and colleagues proposed that the Arg finger promotes GTP hydrolysis in small GTPases by rotating the α-phosphate with respect to β- and γ-phosphates towards an eclipsed conformation.
source: Recently, Gerwert and colleagues proposed that the Arg finger promotes GTP hydrolysis in small GTPases by rotating the α-phosphate with respect to β- and γ-phosphates towards an eclipsed conformation, which would favor the bond cleavage because of repulsion between the oxygen atoms of all three phosphate groups (Rudack et al., 2012; Mann et al., 2016; Gerwert et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rudack et al., 2012; Mann et al., 2016; Gerwert et al., 2017

claim: The eclipsed conformation would favor bond cleavage because of repulsion between the oxygen atoms of all three phosphate groups.
source: Recently, Gerwert and colleagues proposed that the Arg finger promotes GTP hydrolysis in small GTPases by rotating the α-phosphate with respect to β- and γ-phosphates towards an eclipsed conformation, which would favor the bond cleavage because of repulsion between the oxygen atoms of all three phosphate groups (Rudack et al., 2012; Mann et al., 2016; Gerwert et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rudack et al., 2012; Mann et al., 2016; Gerwert et al., 2017

claim: Blackburn and colleagues proposed that the insertion of the activating Arg residue leads to the reshuffling of the hydrogen bonded network, which drives the displacement of the attacking water molecule into the reactive position.
source: Blackburn and colleagues proposed that the insertion of the activating Arg residue leads to the reshuffling of the hydrogen bonded network, which drives the displacement of the attacking water molecule into the reactive position (Jin et al., 2016; Jin et al., 2017a; Jin et al., 2017b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jin et al., 2016; Jin et al., 2017a; Jin et al., 2017b

claim: Some P-loop NTPases functionally depend not on Arg/Lys fingers, but on monovalent cations.
source: Some P-loop NTPases functionally depend not on Arg/Lys fingers, but on monovalent cations (Figure 1B,C, Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1B,C and Supplementary file 1A

claim: Strict dependence on K+ ions was shown for the bacterial tRNA-modifying GTPase MnmE.
source: Strict dependence on K+ ions was shown, among others, for the bacterial tRNA-modifying GTPase MnmE (also known as TrmE), Era-like GTPase Der from Escherichia coli, AtNOS/AtNOA1 GTPase from Arabidopsis thaliana, ribosome assembly GTPase YqeH, G-protein coupled with ferrous transporter FeoB, ribosome-binding ATPase YchF, bacterial ribosome biogenesis protein RgbA, and the DNA repair and recombination protein Rad51 (Wu et al., 2005; Yamanaka et al., 2000; Scrima and Wittinghofer, 2006; Hwang and Inouye, 2001; Moreau et al., 2008; Anand et al., 2010; Ash et al., 2011; Ash et al., 2012; Tomar et al., 2011; Achila et al., 2012; Rice et al., 2001; Liu et al., 2004; Sehorn et al., 2004; Meyer et al., 2009; Böhme et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: The requirement for K+ or NH4+ ions was shown both for the intrinsic and ribosome-dependent GTPase activity of several ubiquitous translation factors.
source: The requirement for K+ or NH4+ ions was shown both for the intrinsic and ribosome-dependent GTPase activity of several ubiquitous translation factors (Conway, 1964; Conway and Lipmann, 1964; Lubin and Ennis, 1964; Fasano et al., 1982; Ebel et al., 1992; Chinali and Parmeggiani, 1980; Dubnoff and Maitra, 1972; Kuhle and Ficner, 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: The dependence on K+ ions was an ancestral trait which was subsequently replaced by the reliance on arginine or lysine fingers.
source: Based on the K+-dependence of several ancient ATPases and GTPases of the TRAFAC class and on phylogenomic analysis, we have previously suggested that the dependence on K+ ions was an ancestral trait which was subsequently replaced by the reliance on arginine or lysine fingers (Mulkidjanian et al., 2012; Dibrova et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mulkidjanian et al., 2012; Dibrova et al., 2015

claim: In K+-dependent P-loop NTPases, the catalytically important K+ ion occupies the position of the positively charged nitrogen atom of the Arg/Lys finger.
source: In K+-dependent P-loop NTPases, the catalytically important K+ ion occupies the position of the positively charged nitrogen atom of the Arg/Lys finger, interacting with the phosphate groups of the NTP molecule from the opposite side of the Mg2+ ion (Scrima and Wittinghofer, 2006; Ash et al., 2012), see also Figure 1.
evidence: Supported by citations to Scrima and Wittinghofer, 2006; Ash et al., 2012 and reference to Figure 1

claim: K+-dependent P-loop NTPases have a specific K+-binding 'K-loop' and two specific Asn/Asp residues in the P-loop.
source: Using crystal structures of several K+-dependent P-loop NTPases, a set of their characteristic features could be identified, including a specific K+-binding 'K-loop' and two specific Asn/Asp residues in the P-loop (Anand et al., 2010; Ash et al., 2012; Mulkidjanian et al., 2012) (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by citations to Anand et al., 2010; Ash et al., 2012; Mulkidjanian et al., 2012 and reference to Figure 1B,C

claim: In the majority of K+-dependent P-loop NTPases, Na+ ions could not replace K+ ions as cofactors.
source: In the majority of K+-dependent P-loop NTPases, Na+ ions could not replace K+ ions as cofactors (Yamanaka et al., 2000; Hwang and Inouye, 2001; Moreau et al., 2008; Tomar et al., 2011; Achila et al., 2012; Böhme et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: The very existence of ubiquitous K+-dependent NTPases, along with the strict dependence of the translation system on cytoplasmic K+ ions and its inhibition by Na+ ions, require maintaining the [K+]/[Na+] ratio >>1.0 in the cytoplasm.
source: The very existence of ubiquitous K+-dependent NTPases, along with the strict dependence of the translation system on cytoplasmic K+ ions and its inhibition by Na+ ions (Lubin and Ennis, 1964), require maintaining the [K+]/[Na+] ratio >>1.0 in the cytoplasm.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lubin and Ennis, 1964 and logical inference

claim: Cells may spend up to a half of the available energy to maintain the proper [K+]/[Na+] ratio.
source: Since Na+ usually prevails over K+ in natural habitats, cells may spend up to a half of the available energy to maintain the proper [K+]/[Na+] ratio (Skulachev, 1978).
evidence: Supported by citation to Skulachev, 1978

claim: Human dynamin and the dynamin-like protein from A. thaliana are equally well activated by Na+ and K+ ions.
source: For P-loop NTPases, the use of Na+ ion as an activating cofactor is, in principle, possible: human dynamin and the dynamin-like protein from A. thaliana are equally well activated by Na+ and K+ ions (Chappie et al., 2010;Yan et al., 2011 ).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chappie et al., 2010; Yan et al., 2011

claim: In dynamins, Na+ ions bind in a similar position to that occupied by K+ ions in potassium-dependent NTPases.
source: The structures of dynamins show that Na+ ions bind in a similar position to that occupied by K+ ions in potassium-dependent NTPases (Ash et al., 2012), cf. Figure 1B and C.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ash et al., 2012 and reference to Figure 1B and C

claim: Larger ions, such as K+ and Rb+, were more efficient than the smaller Na+ and Li+ ions in accelerating transphosphorylation.
source: Back in 1960, larger ions, such as K+ and Rb+, were shown to be more efficient than the smaller Na+ and Li+ ions in accelerating transphosphorylation (Lowenstein, 1960), see Supplementary file 1B.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lowenstein, 1960 and reference to Supplementary file 1B

claim: In MD simulations of the Mg-NTP complexes in water in the presence of K+, Na+, and NH4+ ions, these ions got bound to the phosphate chain in the same two sites that are taken by positive charges in the active sites of P-loop NTPases.
source: We report that, in MD simulations of the Mg-NTP complexes in water in the presence of K+, Na+, and NH4+ ions, these ions (hereafter M+ ions) got bound to the phosphate chain in the same two sites that are taken by positive charges in the active sites of P-loop NTPases, namely, (i) between β- and γ-phosphates, in the position of the amino group of the invariant P-loop lysine residue, and (ii) between α- and γ-phosphates, in the position that is occupied either by the side chain of the activating Arg/Lys finger or by an M+ ion.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data presented in the manuscript

claim: The extended conformation of the phosphate chain was achieved in water only in the presence of the larger K+ and NH4+ ions, but not with the smaller Na+ ions.
source: The extended conformation of the phosphate chain, which is similar to the catalytically prone conformation of tightly bound Mg-NTP complexes in the active sites of diverse P-loop NTPases, was achieved in water only in the presence of the larger K+ and NH4+ ions, but not with the smaller Na+ ions.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data presented in the manuscript

claim: MD simulations of the K+-dependent GTPase MnmE showed that binding of the activating K+ ion between α- and γ-phosphates of an extended triphosphate chain led to the rotation of the γ-phosphate group yielding an almost eclipsed, catalytically productive conformation of the triphosphate chain.
source: The MD simulations of the K+-dependent GTPase MnmE showed that binding of the activating K+ ion between α- and γ-phosphates of an extended triphosphate chain led to the rotation of the γ-phosphate group yielding an almost eclipsed, catalytically productive conformation of the triphosphate chain.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data presented in the manuscript

claim: The activation of K+-dependent NTPases requires a specific interaction of the P-loop domain with the respective activating moiety to shape the cation-binding site.
source: In addition, comparative structural analysis has revealed that, although the activating M+ ions are bound exclusively by the residues of the P-loop NTPase domain, the activation of respective NTPases additionally requires a specific interaction of the P-loop domain with the respective activating moiety (another protein domain or an RNA/DNA molecule) to shape the cation-binding site.
evidence: Supported by comparative structural analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: The mechanism of requiring specific interaction with activating partners prevents uncontrolled hydrolysis of the cellular NTP stock.
source: Such a mechanism prevents uncontrolled hydrolysis of the cellular NTP stock, which, otherwise, could cause cell death.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the structural and functional data

claim: M+ ions formed coordination bonds with oxygen atoms of the ATP phosphate chain with respective lengths of 2.2 Å for Na+, 2.6 Å for K+, and 2.7 Å for NH4+ ions.
source: Distance distributions obtained from the MD simulation data (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) show that M+ ions formed coordination bonds with oxygen atoms of the ATP phosphate chain with the respective lengths of 2.2 Å for Na+, 2.6 Å for K+, and 2.7 Å for NH4+ ions.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: These coordination bond distances correspond well with the crystallographic data for these ions.
source: These distances correspond well with the crystallographic data for these ions (Harding, 2002; Harding, 2004; Sigel et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Harding, 2002; Harding, 2004; Sigel et al., 2016

claim: On time average, within the 4 Å radius around the phosphate chain, 1.5 cations were present in the case of Na+ and NH4+, and 0.75 cations were present in the case of K+.
source: On time average, within the 4 Å radius around the phosphate chain, 1.5 cations were present in the case of Na+ and NH4+, and 0.75 cations were present in the case of K+ (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: At least two distinct binding sites for M+ ions could be identified: one formed by the oxygen atoms of β- and γ-phosphates (BG site), and the other involving the oxygens of α- and γ-phosphates (AG site).
source: Based on the radial distributions of M+ ions around each individual oxygen atom of the ATP phosphate chain (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and visual inspection of the M+ binding to the phosphate groups, at least two distinct binding sites for M+ ions could be identified (Figure 2A). One of them was formed by the oxygen atoms of β- and γ-phosphates, and the other site involved the oxygens of α- and γ-phosphates. We refer to these binding sites as the BG and AG sites, respectively.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: For each M+ ion, MD simulation data indicated much lower occupancy of the AG site than of the BG site.
source: For each M+ ion, MD simulation data indicated much lower occupancy of the AG site than of the BG site; the average occupancy of the BG site was estimated to be 0.95 for Na+, 0.72 for NH4+, and 0.5 for K+, compared to the average occupancy of the AG site of 0.15 for Na+, 0.2 for NH4+, and 0.05 for K+ (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 2C–E

claim: Binding of the second K+ ion in the AG site was found to stabilize all three phosphate groups in a near-eclipsed conformation.
source: Binding of the second K+ ion in the AG site was found to stabilize all three phosphate groups in a near-eclipsed conformation, with the phosphorus-oxygen bonds of the α-phosphate group almost coplanar to the respective bonds of β- and γ-phosphates (Figure 3; Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 3 and Supplementary file 1D

claim: Binding of the second K+ ion in the AG site promotes the transition of the phosphate chain into the almost fully eclipsed conformation by approximately 27 meV or 2.5 kJ/mol.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, binding of the second K+ ion in the AG site promotes the transition of the phosphate chain into the almost fully eclipsed conformation by approximately 27 meV or 2.5 kJ/mol.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Cleavage of the bond between β- and γ-phosphates is believed to proceed via a planar transition complex, whereby the PB-O3B-PG angle widens.
source: Cleavage of the bond between β- and γ-phosphates is believed to proceed via a planar transition complex, whereby the PB-O3B-PG angle widens (Kamerlin et al., 2013; Jin et al., 2017a; Jin et al., 2017b; Kiani and Fischer, 2016; Warshel and Prasad, 2017; Akola and Jones, 2003; Grigorenko et al., 2006; Harrison and Schulten, 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: While all M+ ions seemed to contract the phosphate chain, it was more extended in the presence of K+ ions than in the presence of NH4+ or Na+ ions.
source: While all M+ ions seemed to contract the phosphate chain, it was more extended in the presence of K+ ions than in the presence of NH4+ or Na+ ions.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data presented in the manuscript

claim: Na+ and NH4+ ions could induce an even more compressed, curled conformation of the Mg-ATP complex with even shorter distances between PA and PG atoms.
source: Furthermore, Na+ and NH4+ ions could induce an even more compressed, curled conformation of the Mg-ATP complex with even shorter distances between PA and PG atoms.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data presented in the manuscript

claim: Such curled conformations of the phosphate chain were not observed either in the presence of K+ ions or in the absence of M+ ions.
source: Such curled conformations of the phosphate chain were not observed either in the presence of K+ ions or in the absence of M+ ions (Figure 4, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 4 and Table 1

claim: The conformational space of phosphate chain conformations, as seen in P-loop NTPases, overlapped much better with conformations seen in the MD simulations of Mg-ATP with K+ and NH4+ ions than with conformations obtained with Na+ ions.
source: Altogether, Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 show that the conformational space of phosphate chain conformations, as seen in P-loop NTPases, overlapped much better with conformations seen in the MD simulations of Mg-ATP with K+ and NH4+ ions than with conformations obtained with Na+ ions.
evidence: Supported by comparison of MD simulation data with crystal structures shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: The binding sites for M+ ions observed in the MD simulations were exactly those occupied by positively charged groups in the structures of P-loop NTPases.
source: Figure 6 shows that the binding sites for M+ ions observed in the MD simulations (Figure 6A) were exactly those occupied by positively charged groups in the structures of P-loop NTPases (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: Supported by comparison of MD simulation data with crystal structures shown in Figure 6

claim: The binding site between the β- and γ-phosphates (the BG site) is always occupied by the amino group of the conserved P-loop lysine residue.
source: The binding site between the β- and γ-phosphates (the BG site) is always occupied by the amino group of the conserved P-loop lysine residue, whereas the binding site between the α- and γ-phosphates (the AG site) could be occupied, in the crystal structures, by either a K+ or Na+ ion (Figure 6B), or an amino group of an activating lysine residue, or the guanidinium group of arginine (Figure 6C), or a water molecule (see below).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 6

claim: In all analyzed structures of diverse P-loop NTPases, the conserved P-loop motif keeps the triphosphate chain of bound NTPs in an extended, catalytically prone conformation.
source: In all analyzed structures of diverse P-loop NTPases, the conserved P-loop motif keeps the triphosphate chain of bound NTPs (or their analogs) in an extended, catalytically prone conformation, similar to that imposed on NTPs in water by potassium or ammonium ions.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: In all P-loop NTPases, the phosphate chain is seen in the extended conformation similar to that observed in the presence K+ and NH4+ but not Na+ ions.
source: In all P-loop NTPases, the phosphate chain is seen in the extended conformation similar to that observed in the presence K+ and NH4+ but not Na+ ions (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by comparison of structural data with MD simulations shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: The extended conformation is stabilized by numerous interactions of all three phosphate groups with the residues of the P-loop motif.
source: Such an extended conformation is known to be stabilized by numerous interactions of all three phosphate groups with the residues of the P-loop motif, see (Wittinghofer and Vetter, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wittinghofer and Vetter, 2011

claim: Binding in the catalytic site of a P-loop NTPase imposes constraints on the Mg-NTP complex, so that only particular conformations of the phosphate chain are allowed.
source: Binding in the catalytic site of a P-loop NTPase imposes constraints on the Mg-NTP complex, so that only particular conformations of the phosphate chain are allowed.
evidence: Based on structural knowledge and inference

claim: NTP binding to an inactive P-loop domain increases the rate constant of hydrolysis by several orders of magnitude as compared to the NTP hydrolysis in water.
source: These conformations appear to be catalytically prone, since NTP binding to an inactive P-loop domain (in the absence of a specific activating protein) already increases the rate constant of hydrolysis by several orders of magnitude as compared to the NTP hydrolysis in water (Kötting and Gerwert, 2004; Shutes and Der, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kötting and Gerwert, 2004; Shutes and Der, 2006

claim: In the top row of Figure 5, the heat maps included all conformations of Mg-ATP in water, including those not found in crystal structures of P-loop NTPases.
source: In the top row of Figure 5, the heat maps included all conformations of Mg-ATP in water, including those not found in crystal structures of P-loop NTPases, for example with αβγ coordination of Mg2+, as shown in Figure 4.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 4

claim: Conformations of Mg-ATP complexes from MD simulations only partially overlaped with the conformations of non-hydrolyzable analogs of NTPs in P-loop NTPases.
source: Therefore, conformations of Mg-ATP complexes from MD simulations only partially overlaped with the conformations of non-hydrolyzable analogs of NTPs in P-loop NTPases (the blue contours in Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by comparison shown in Figure 5A

claim: The extent of the overlap between MD simulations and crystal structures depended on the nature of the cation used in MD simulations: it was highest with K+ and lowest with Na+.
source: The extent of the overlap depended on the nature of the cation used in MD simulations: it was highest with K+ and lowest with Na+.
evidence: Supported by comparison of MD simulation data with crystal structures

claim: In the presence of K+ ions, the occurrence of transition state-like conformations was notably higher, while in simulations with Na+ such conformations were completely absent.
source: Still, in the presence of K+ ions, the occurrence of such transition state-like conformations was notably higher, while in simulations with Na+ such conformations were completely absent.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data

claim: In the absence of any M+, the phosphate chain was remarkably elongated, displaying large PA-PG distances that were not observed either in simulations with added cations or in crystal structures.
source: As seen on the heat maps, in the absence of any M+, the phosphate chain was remarkably elongated, displaying large PA-PG distances that were not observed either in simulations with added cations or in crystal structures.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data and comparison with crystal structures

claim: The presence of M+ ions led to the shortening of the PA-PG distances.
source: The presence of M+ ions led to the shortening of the PA-PG distances.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data

claim: In the simulations with Na+ ions, the ATP phosphate chain was more contracted than in the crystal structures of P-loop NTPases.
source: In the simulations with Na+ ions, the ATP phosphate chain was more contracted than in the crystal structures of P-loop NTPases (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by comparison of MD simulation data with crystal structures shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: In the MD simulations with K+ and NH4+ ions, the phosphate chain shape matched almost exactly the conformations of the NTP analogs in the structures of P-loop NTPases.
source: In contrast, in the MD simulations with K+ and NH4+ ions, the phosphate chain shape matched almost exactly the conformations of the NTP analogs in the structures of P-loop NTPases.
evidence: Supported by comparison of MD simulation data with crystal structures

claim: In MD simulations in the presence of K+ and NH4+ ions, the distribution of the conformations of Mg-ATP complex spread over the areas of non-hydrolyzable NTP analogs and covered even transition state analogs.
source: In MD simulations in the presence of K+ and NH4+ ions, the distribution of the conformations of Mg-ATP complex spread over the areas of non-hydrolyzable NTP analogs and covered even transition state analogs (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Only the conformations of the transition state analogs with severely widened (>135°) PB-O3B-PG angle were not matched by the MD-derived conformations.
source: Only the conformations of the transition state analogs with severely widened (>135°) PB-O3B-PG angle were not matched by the MD-derived conformations.
evidence: Supported by comparison of MD simulation data with crystal structures

claim: In all available structures of K+-dependent P-loop NTPases, the conserved P-loop motif keeps the triphosphate chain of bound NTPs in an extended, catalytically prone conformation.
source: In all analyzed structures of diverse P-loop NTPases, the conserved P-loop motif keeps the triphosphate chain of bound NTPs (or their analogs) in an extended, catalytically prone conformation, similar to that imposed on NTPs in water by potassium or ammonium ions.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: In total, 17 structures of cation-dependent P-loop NTPases in complex with NTP analogs and K+, Na+, or NH4+ ions bound in the active site were identified and analyzed.
source: In total, we were able to identify and analyze 17 structures of cation-dependent P-loop NTPases in complex with NTP analogs and K+, Na+, or NH4+ ions bound in the active site (Table 3).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis presented in Table 3

claim: In all analyzed structures of cation-dependent P-loop NTPases, the distances between PA and PG atoms were in the range of 4.9–5.3 Å for the non-hydrolyzable analogs and 5.3–5.6 Å for transition state analogs.
source: For each such structure, we checked the shape of the phosphate chain and the coordination sphere of the cation in the AG site. In all these structures, the distances between PA and PG atoms (or between the corresponding mimicking atoms) were in the range of 4.9–5.3 Å for the non-hydrolyzable analogs and 5.3–5.6 Å for transition state analogs (Table 3).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis presented in Table 3

claim: These PA-PG distance values are similar to the PA-PG distances observed in MD simulations of the Mg-ATP complex in the presence of K+ ions.
source: These values are similar to the PA-PG distances observed in MD simulations of the Mg-ATP complex in the presence of K+ ions (Figures 4 and 5 and Table 1).
evidence: Supported by comparison of structural data with MD simulation data shown in Figures 4 and 5 and Table 1

claim: Very few structures of K+-dependent GTPases of the TRAFAC class contained K+ ions in their AG sites.
source: To our surprise, very few structures of K+-dependent GTPases of the TRAFAC class contained K+ ions in their AG sites (cf Supplementary file 1A and Table 3).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis presented in Supplementary file 1A and Table 3

claim: In most cases, the K+ loops were either unresolved or distorted in structures of K+-dependent GTPases.
source: Furthermore, in most cases, the K+ loops were either unresolved or distorted (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: During the catalytic turnover, two MnmE proteins undergo conformational changes to allow dimerization of their P-loop GTPase domains resulting in their mutual activation.
source: It is believed that during the catalytic turnover, two MnmE proteins undergo conformational changes to allow dimerization of their P-loop GTPase domains (G-domains) resulting in their mutual activation (Meyer et al., 2009; Böhme et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Meyer et al., 2009; Böhme et al., 2010

claim: In the crystallized full-length MnmE dimer, the K-loops are not resolved, and no K+ binding is observed.
source: In the crystallized full-length MnmE dimer, only the N-terminal domains of the two proteins interact, forming a central hinge, whereas the large helical domains and G-domains are located on the opposite sides from the central hinge (PDB: 3GEI, Figure 6—figure supplement 2). In such an arrangement, the distance between the active sites of the G-domains (with non-hydrolyzable GTP analogs bound) is about 20 Å (Scrima and Wittinghofer, 2006; Sehorn et al., 2004). evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and citations to Scrima and Wittinghofer, 2006; Sehorn et al., 2004
